hlido_opinion.headline: A 13-chapter teardown that rebuilds a coding agent in ~5,000 lines — genuinely useful as education, and explicit that it is not a product.
hlido_opinion.body: This is a tutorial repository, and its honesty about that is the reason it scores as well as it does. The captured documentation walks 13 chapters from an empty loop to a working coding agent in roughly 5,000 lines, in both TypeScript and Python, covering the agent loop, a 13-tool system, system-prompt engineering, CLI and session handling, streaming with two backends, a permission model, context management, then memory, skills, plan mode, multi-agent and MCP integration. Two things lift it above the usual 'build X from scratch' genre. First, every code chapter is stated to be runnable without an API key, which removes the main reason such tutorials rot unread. Second, it carries a side-by-side architecture comparison against Claude Code that works in the right direction — 66+ tools versus 13, a four-stage compression pipeline versus four layers, seven permission layers with AST analysis versus five modes with declarative rules, 500k+ lines versus ~5,500 — so a reader learns where the simplification was made rather than being told the small version is equivalent. The disclaimer is equally clear: it follows Claude Code's publicly observable behaviour, does not claim to match the real internals, and states no affiliation with Anthropic, whose trademark it names. The limits follow from the purpose. This is not a maintained product, carries no support posture, and most of the documentation is in Chinese with only partial English, which narrows the audience it can actually teach.

tier_rationale: STEADY (75) because three of five surface checks passed and the public surface does what it claims: a specific chapter structure, runnable code per chapter, a concrete architecture comparison with the thing it is modelled on, and an unambiguous scope disclaimer. Not VITAL because it is explicitly a learning project rather than something to deploy — no support, no stability commitment, no production evidence — and the predominantly Chinese documentation limits who can use it.
what_it_does_well: Every code chapter is stated to run without an API key — removes the usual barrier to actually following along
Architecture comparison against Claude Code is specific and candid about what was simplified away
Two complete implementations (TypeScript and Python) rather than pseudocode
Scope disclaimer is explicit: publicly observable behaviour only, no claimed parity, no Anthropic affiliation
Covers the parts most tutorials skip — permissions, context compression, memory recall, MCP over stdio
Documented CLI flags map to real operational concerns (cost caps, turn limits, plan mode, CI mode)
what_it_fails_at: Educational project, not a maintained product — no support, SLA or stability commitment
Documentation is predominantly Chinese; English coverage is partial, limiting the audience
No production or reliability evidence, by design
Simplified against the real thing by its own comparison table (13 tools vs 66+, 5 permission modes vs 7 layers)
Depends on third-party model APIs the project does not control
best_for: Engineers who want to understand coding-agent internals without reading a 500k-line codebase
Teams building their own agent harness who need a reference implementation to study
Anyone evaluating what a minimal viable coding agent actually requires
not_recommended_for: Production use — it is a tutorial and says so
Teams needing vendor support or a maintenance guarantee
Anyone looking for Claude Code parity; the project explicitly disclaims it
red_flags: Names and benchmarks itself against a third party's trademarked product; the disclaimer is present and clear, but the dependency on that framing is structural

compared_to.verdict_diff: Claude Code is the production agent this project reconstructs for teaching, and the repo's own table concedes the gap (66+ tools vs 13, 500k+ lines vs ~5,500). Use Claude Code to do work; use this to understand how such a thing is built.

Aider is a maintained open-source coding agent you can read AND run in production. This project is smaller and purely instructional. Aider when you want working software whose source you can study; this when the lesson is the point.
OpenCode is a production-intent open-source terminal agent. This repository teaches the architecture such an agent needs. Complementary: read this, then deploy one of those.
